abstract: "*All children with Down syndrome experience delays in language development. By estimating typical trajectories of vocabulary development we can offer families and practitioners insights into expected ranges and rates of progress. These can help to inform teaching goals and methods, and to identify children experiencing more complex or challenging difficulties. This study aims to provide accurate estimates of typical trajectories of word learning and distributions of expected spoken and understood word counts at six monthly intervals for children with Down syndrome aged 12 months to 6 years.*"

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Children with Down syndrome experience difficulties learning language [@naessLanguageVerbalShortterm2011; @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020] and this adversely impacts many aspect of their lives. They learn the meanings of words and learn to say words more slowly than most other children [@naessDifferencesSimilaritiesPredictors2021]. Learning vocabulary is a foundational skill: it is important for learning broader language skills, including grammar, and for learning to read [@naessReadingSkillsChildren2012; @hulmeGrowthReadingSkills2012].

Parents and practitioners working with people with Down syndrome report that past research has not focussed enough on practical issues that might make meaningful differences to their lives, leading to calls for researchers to makes it easier for families and educators to access evidence-based information to inform decisions related to real life issues [@cristescuShapeResearchChange2024]. In our experience, families and educators are interested in information about vocabulary development in children with Down syndrome, including the range of words understood or spoken at different ages, rates of word learning, and the range of ages at which a minimum number of words may be learned. Answers to questions about vocabulary development are of relevance to everyday teaching practice and early intervention. They may alleviate unwarranted concerns about slow progress and may also help to identify children experiencing additional or more complex difficulties. They can also inform teaching recommendations – for example, by estimating the range of ages within which most children are expected to attain specific skills.

## Study aims

This study therefore aims to describe the development of vocabulary knowledge in children with Down syndrome with a focus on interpretable statistics that can inform teaching and support. Specifically, we aim to:

- Characterise trajectories of word learning, and spoken and signed production among children with Down syndrome aged 12 months to 6 years
- Estimate the ranges of words understood, signed or spoken by with Down syndrome at 6-monthly intervals from 12 to 72 months.
- Identify the proportions of children with Down syndrome reaching specific vocabulary milestones at different ages
- Contrast vocabulary development among children with Down syndrome with that among typical development

## A large dataset

Accurate estimates of trends in vocabulary development over time and distributions of words learned at particular ages require many observations of many children.

The precision of an estimated average improves only with the square root of the number of observations [@gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020, chapter 16; @wainerMostDangerousEquation2007]. Therefore, halving uncertainty requires four times the data. Put another way, an estimate resting on 300 observations is about three times more precise than one resting on 30.

Estimates from small samples also differ from each other more than estimates from large samples do (are more prone to sampling error) [@bergmannPromotingReplicabilityDevelopmental2018; @schubertImprovingStatisticalReporting2025]. For example, if the spread between children at a given age has standard deviation $\sigma$, the average estimated from $n$ children typically misses the truth by $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Therefore, two studies of 20 children each will typically report averages about a third of the whole between-child spread apart ($\sqrt{2},\sigma/\sqrt{n}$) through chance alone, before any real difference between their samples, settings or measures is counted. A recent review of studies of vocabulary among children with a variety of developmental conditions identified 17 studies of children with Down syndrome with sample sizes ranging from 6 to 40 (median 25) [@laudanskaCommunicativeDevelopmentInventories2026].

Sample sizes matter even more for characterising trajectories. A trajectory incorporates many estimates: average word counts at each age are estimated from nearby observations, so the data are divided among the ages they describe. With tens of observations in total most ages would rest on a handful of children. Moreover, the quantities of most practical value are ranges rather than averages. These are properties of the spread between children, estimated from differences among children. Spread required more data than an average does and statements about the edges of a range depend on the children observed least often.

To maximise the accuracy of our estimates we pool parent reports of words learned by children with Down syndrome from 14 studies in 6 countries. For comparisons, we pool parent reports of words learned by children without identified difficulties (‘typically developing’) from XX studies in XX countries.

## Statistical modelling and Bayesian inference

To identify trajectories and to estimate expected ranges of word learning, we develop statistical models that describe how children's vocabulary grows over time and how it varies between individuals.

Statistical modelling and inference provide methods for defining mathematical models and evaluating them against data to obtain evidence-based estimates of the parameters of interest [@coxPrinciplesStatisticalInference2006; @gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020; @chanStatisticalModelingComputation2025]. They are central to evaluating scientific theories and interpreting data, and can express what a theory means more precisely than words alone [@farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018, chapter 1].

A statistical model is a set of assumptions describing a process that could generate the data, relating the parameters of interest to what we observe. Because a model can also generate synthetic datasets consistent with those assumptions, we can simulate from it to check that it behaves as intended [@farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. Statistical inference then uses the model and the observed data to estimate its unknown parameters, test specific claims, predict future observations, and quantify how uncertain those conclusions are.

### Statistical models

Statistical models do not by themselves explain how the world works, though they can evaluate the predictions of models that do. A regression model reveals statistical relationships between predictors and outcomes, but those relationships acquire their real-world relevance only within an *empirical model* — an account of the real-world phenomenon that informs which statistical and process models can test it [@spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @vanoijenBayesianCompendium2024;@farrellComputationalModelingCognition2018].

The mapping between the two runs both ways: one empirical model admits many statistical models, and one statistical model is consistent with many empirical models. So even when a statistical model fits the observed data well, we cannot be certain its motivating explanation is ‘the right one’ — another, equally credible, explanation may fit just as well:

> "Many models correspond to the same hypothesis, and many hypotheses correspond to a single model. This makes strict falsification impossible." [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020, page 4]

Developing and evaluating models is therefore continual and iterative: a competing model may explain the data better, and new observations refine existing models, revise theories and motivate new ones [@gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026].

### Bayesian inference

There are different approaches to statistical inference, differing in their philosophical and mathematical foundations and in the conclusions they license [@gelmanBayesianDataAnalysis2013; @wakefieldBayesianFrequentistRegression2013; @spanosProbabilityTheoryStatistical2019; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. Bayesian methods remain uncommon in developmental Down syndrome research, but for the questions this study addresses they offer four concrete advantages: probability statements that mean what most people take them to mean; uncertainty expressed as full distributions; a principled way to bring existing knowledge to bear; and direct predictions about individual children.

#### Probability as uncertainty

Bayesian inference treats probability as a measure of uncertainty about unknown quantities -- "relative, in part to this ignorance, in part to our knowledge" [@laplaceEssaiPhilosophiqueProbabilites1814] -- so that a number near one marks an event we consider very likely and one near zero an event we consider very unlikely [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. On a partly cloudy day, "a 50% chance of rain this afternoon" means that, given what we currently know, rain and no rain seem about equally plausible.

#### Estimates as distributions

Bayesian inference begins with a prior distribution -- what we consider plausible before seeing the data -- and uses Bayes' theorem to update it into a posterior distribution that combines prior and data, with uncertainty built in and shown by how peaked or flat the posterior is [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024].

@fig-bayes-update-20 illustrates this. For a yes/no outcome we begin with a weakly informative prior centred on $p = 0.5$ (blue), expecting all-yes or all-no to be less likely than intermediate values. We then observe 20 simulated outcomes, 11 of them "yes" (green), and apply Bayes' theorem to obtain the posterior (orange). With only 20 observations the sample is not centred on the true mean ($p_\text{obs} = 0.55$, $p_\text{true} = 0.65$); this weak prior shifts and narrows the posterior only slightly, leaving it primarily data-driven ($p_\text{post} = 0.54$).

![**Bayesian updating** ($n = 20$). Given a prior distribution (blue) and the observed data (green), we use Bayes theorem to obtain the posterior distribution (orange).](figures/bayes_update.png){#fig-bayes-update-20}

@fig-bayes-update-100 repeats this with the same prior and true mean but 100 observations: the observed mean is closer to the truth ($p_\text{obs} = 0.61$) and the posterior is more concentrated around it ($p_\text{post} = 0.61$).

![**Bayesian updating** ($n = 100$). As @fig-bayes-update-20, but with 100 observations: the posterior distribution is now more concentrated around the observed mean.](figures/bayes_update_2.png){#fig-bayes-update-100}

Frequentist uncertainty is instead grounded in how an estimation procedure behaves across repeated samples; a confidence interval is not a probability statement about where the true value lies and does not rank some values as more plausible than others [@moreyFallacyPlacingConfidence2016] -- a distinction that is, unfortunately, often misinterpreted in practice [@hoekstraRobustMisinterpretationConfidence2014]. A Bayesian posterior instead supports direct statements such as: "given our model and the data, the typical 36-month-old child with Down syndrome learns about 5 new words per month, with an 89% probability that the median rate lies between 2 and 7." These are the statements families, practitioners and researchers tend to find useful -- and, as McElreath observes, the ones "scientists tend to project onto statistical results" in any case [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. Bayesian inference is also logically coherent and well suited to complex models [@bernardoBayesianStatistics2025; @wagenmakersBayesianInferencePsychology2018; @wagenmakersBayesianFrequentistInference2008].

#### Using existing knowledge

A prior encodes what is plausible about each parameter before the current data are analysed. Priors can draw on previous research and the experience of people with relevant expertise, or be weakly informative -- ruling out implausible values while letting the data lead. A well-grounded prior combined with the data yields estimates that are more stable, and often more precise, than the data alone -- especially valuable when datasets are small or noisy and a substantial evidence base already exists.

The need to specify a prior is sometimes criticised as "subjective". But every analysis rests on assumptions; the Bayesian ones are simply explicit and open to scrutiny. A prior "should be chosen, evaluated, and revised just like all of the other components of the model" [@mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020], and we can test directly how sensitive our estimates are to it [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020]. For this study, priors let us bring existing knowledge of vocabulary development to bear and improve the accuracy of our estimates.

#### Predictions for individual children

From the posterior we can also predict unobserved outcomes. Drawing parameter values from the posterior and simulating a new observation for each draw yields a *posterior predictive distribution* that carries both the randomness in the data and our uncertainty about the parameters. This supports statements such as: "given our model and the data, there is an 89% probability that a 36-month-old child with Down syndrome understands between 0 and 142 words" -- directly useful for setting expectations about individual children.

#### Computation

Bayesian inference is centuries old [@bayesLIIEssaySolving1763; @LaplaceMemoireProbabilite; @laplaceTheorieAnalytiqueProbabilites1820] but became practical for all but the simplest models only with modern sampling algorithms [@metropolisEquationStateCalculations1953; @hastingsMonteCarloSampling1970; @hoffmanNoUTurnSamplerAdaptively2014], now packaged in accessible open-source tools such as Stan and PyMC with interfaces to R and Python [@standevelopmentteamStanLanguageReference2026; @abril-plaPyMCModernComprehensive2023]. It is consequently now used across economics, political science, ecology, biology, neuroscience, medicine, psychology and education research [@gillBayesianModelingInference2020; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020; @bonBeingBayesian2020s2023; @pfadtMethodologicalMetamorphosisRapid2025].

#### Conclusions

A goal of this study is to provide interpretable statistics that can accurately inform expectations, intervention and teaching practice. Empirical and statistical modelling with Bayesian inference let us estimate word-learning trajectories with intuitive uncertainty statements, and simulate predicted outcomes for children with Down syndrome at different ages, to offer relevant and practical insights for families and educators.
